title: U.S. Senate · Alaska

context.text: Alaska uses a top-four nonpartisan primary followed by ranked-choice voting in the general election. In the August 18, 2026 primary, Mary Peltola (D) placed first with 49.5%, incumbent Daniel S. Sullivan (R) placed second with 41.4%, and Dan Sullivan (R), a retired teacher who shares the incumbent's name, placed third with 2.5%. Fourth-place finisher David Leslie (D) withdrew ahead of the August 31, 2026 deadline, so fifth-place finisher Gerald Heikes (R) advanced to the general election instead.

The Alaska Division of Elections initially sought to remove Dan Sullivan from the ballot after the National Republican Senatorial Committee alleged he entered the race to confuse voters and draw votes from the incumbent; Sullivan denied the accusation. An Alaska Superior Court judge ruled he must remain on the ballot, and on June 29, 2026 the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that he could not be removed.

candidates.name: Daniel S. Sullivan

summary.text: Daniel S. Sullivan is the Republican incumbent seeking re-election to a third term in the U.S. Senate. A Marine Corps officer and lawyer by training, he served in the George W. Bush administration and as Alaska Attorney General and Commissioner of Natural Resources before winning the Senate seat in 2014. According to his campaign website, he is running on his record of delivering results for Alaska, including energy development, defense investment and health care.

background.text: Earned a B.A. in economics from Harvard University in 1987 and a joint law degree and Master of Science in Foreign Service from Georgetown University in 1993.

Joined the U.S. Marine Corps in 1993 and moved from active duty to the reserves in 1997 as an infantry and reconnaissance officer. He was recalled to active duty in 2004 as a staff officer to the commander of U.S. Central Command and in July 2013 to serve with a Joint Task Force in Afghanistan, and retired on Feb. 1, 2024 as a Colonel in the Marine Corps Reserve.

Worked as a judicial law clerk for Judge Andrew Kleinfeld of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in 1997 and for Alaska Supreme Court Chief Justice Warren Matthews in 1998, then practiced corporate transactions and commercial litigation at the Anchorage law firm Perkins Coie.

Served in the George W. Bush administration as a director in the International Economics Directorate of the National Security Council staff and later as U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Economic, Energy, and Business Affairs.

Was appointed Alaska Attorney General by Gov. Sarah Palin in June 2009. In December 2010 Gov. Sean Parnell appointed him Commissioner of the Alaska Department of Natural Resources, a post he held until 2013.

Won the 2014 Republican primary for U.S. Senate over Mead Treadwell, Joe Miller and John Jaramillo, then defeated incumbent Democrat Mark Begich in the general election. He was sworn in on January 6, 2015, and won re-election in 2020.

Serves on the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation; Armed Services; Environment and Public Works; and Veterans' Affairs committees, chairing subcommittees on Readiness and Management Support and on Coast Guard, Maritime, and Fisheries (2025-2026 assignments). His official biography also lists him as Chairman of the International Republican Institute.

Awards listed by Ballotpedia include the Defense Meritorious Service Medal, a White House Fellowship (2002), the National Security Council Outstanding Service Award and the U.S. Junior Chamber of Commerce Ten Outstanding Young Americans Award.
According to his official biography, he married Julie Fate Sullivan in 1994 in her hometown of Fairbanks, Alaska, and they have three daughters.

priorities.text: Running on his Senate record, citing tax cuts, reduced regulation, energy development, military and national defense investment, and Alaska's healthcare system.
An "all-of-the-above" energy strategy, which his campaign says supports jobs and high environmental standards.
Reducing fisheries bycatch to protect Alaska's coastal communities.

positions.summary: Is an original cosponsor of the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act, which would bar federal funds to schools that allow transgender girls and women to compete in sports designated for women or girls.
positions.quote: I’m proud to be an original cosponsor of the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act

record.text: Serves on the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, the Armed Services Committee, the Environment and Public Works Committee, and the Veterans' Affairs Committee in the 119th Congress (2025-2026).
Says he introduced the Bycatch Reduction Act to address fisheries bycatch in Alaska waters.

candidates.name: Mary Peltola
candidates.currentRole: Former U.S. Representative, Alaska At-Large District (2022-2025)

summary.text: Mary Peltola is the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. A Bethel-area fisheries and community-development professional, she served in the Alaska House of Representatives (1999-2009), on the Bethel City Council, and as Alaska's at-large U.S. Representative (2022-2025). Her campaign website says she is running to put Alaska first, with a focus on lower costs, fisheries and what she calls fixing a rigged system in Washington.

background.text: Was born in Alaska and graduated from Bethel Regional High School. According to her campaign website, she grew up on the Kuskokwim River fishing salmon with her father.

Her career includes working as a commercial fisher, as a lobbyist with Sattler Strategies, as manager of community development and sustainability with Donlin Gold, and with the Kuskokwim River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission as its executive director.
Served in the Alaska House of Representatives for District 39 (1999-2003) and District 38 (2003-2009).

Served on the Bethel City Council from 2011 to 2013. She has also served on the Orutsararmiut Native Council Tribal Court and the boards of the Nature Conservancy, the Alaska Humanities Forum, the Alaska Children's Trust and the Russian Orthodox Sacred Sites in Alaska.
Won the 2022 special election to fill the at-large U.S. House seat left vacant by Don Young, winning in the second round of ranked-choice counting, and won the full term in the 2022 general election.

Served on the House Natural Resources and Transportation and Infrastructure committees in 2023-2024. She lost her 2024 re-election bid to Nicholas Begich in the third round of ranked-choice counting and left office in January 2025.
Says on her campaign website that she and her husband Buzzy raised seven children in the Kuskokwim region.

priorities.text: Fully funding fish stock assessments so catch limits are based on accurate data rather than what her campaign calls guesswork.
Lowering shipping costs for rural Alaska by restoring funding for Bypass Mail and creating an Essential Freight Service.
Twelve-year congressional term limits, which her campaign describes as a way to stop career politicians corrupted by special interests.

positions.summary: Her campaign's affordability plan proposes eliminating federal income tax for working- and middle-class Alaskans earning under $92,000, paid for by raising taxes on millionaires and billionaires.
positions.quote: paid for by raising taxes on millionaires and billionaires

positions.summary: Her campaign energy plan calls for restoring federal tax credits for solar, wind and hydropower projects and also for oil and gas development in Alaska.
positions.quote: fight to restore federal tax credits for solar, wind, hydropower projects

record.text: As a member of the U.S. House representing Alaska's at-large district, served on the Committee on Natural Resources and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure (Aviation Subcommittee) in the 118th Congress (2023-2024).

candidates.name: Gerald Heikes

summary.text: Gerald "Tap" Heikes is a Republican who has run in several Alaska elections, including the 2014 Republican primary for governor. He placed fifth, with 1% of the vote, in the August 2026 top-four primary and advanced to the general election after David Leslie withdrew.

background.text: Sought the Republican nomination for Alaska governor in the August 19, 2014 primary, finishing behind incumbent Sean Parnell, who defeated Heikes and two other challengers.

Has also appeared on Alaska ballots for the U.S. House at-large seat, including as a write-in candidate in 2020, according to Ballotpedia. Ballotpedia notes he did not complete its Candidate Connection survey in 2020.
Received 1% of the vote in the August 18, 2026 U.S. Senate top-four primary and advanced to the general election when fourth-place finisher David Leslie withdrew before the Aug. 31 deadline.

priorities.text: In a 2024 Alaska Beacon questionnaire, asked what Alaska's biggest need is, he answered: "Is to get out of the federal government control, exercise the states rights through our state constitution."
In the same 2024 questionnaire, asked what Congress should do on immigration, he answered: "Enforcing the law, protecting the borders."

candidates.researchNotes: He did not respond to the 2026 Alaska Beacon voter guide, and no 2026 campaign website or interview was found. Positions are not recorded because the only statements are from his 2024 Alaska Beacon questionnaire for the U.S. House race and are dated as such. His 2024 answer on Israel concerned U.S. support generally rather than military aid and is not included.

candidates.name: Dan Sullivan

summary.text: Dan J. Sullivan is a retired teacher from Petersburg, Alaska, who shares his name with the incumbent senator and placed third in the August 2026 primary with 2.5%. The Alaska Division of Elections removed him from the primary ballot over allegations he entered the race to confuse voters; he denied this, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled on June 29, 2026 that he must remain on the ballot. He told Alaska Public Media he is running because of dissatisfaction with the incumbent and cited affordable housing, health care access and cost of living as his issues.

background.text: Is a retired teacher and lives in Petersburg, Alaska, where he told Alaska Public Media he has lived for decades.
Spent 15 years working for the U.S. Forest Service, according to Alaska Public Media.

Was originally a member of the Alaska Independence Party and, after it dissolved in 2025, joined the Republican Party. He appeared on the primary ballot as "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr." without a party designation, and Ballotpedia lists him as having no party affiliation.

In June 2026 the Alaska Division of Elections removed him from the primary ballot after Republicans, including the incumbent, alleged he was running dishonestly. He denied the accusation, sued, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled on June 29, 2026 that he could appear on the ballot.
Says he supports Alaska's ranked-choice and open-primary system and told Alaska Public Media he wants to appeal to Republican voters critical of the Trump administration.

priorities.text: "Of greatest importance now is housing and affordability, two factors that will keep our young people and elderly from moving South."
"Housing, healthcare and high fuel costs are immediate needs that I see my community struggle with."
"The war in Iran was ill-conceived and poorly planned. I do not support it."

positions.summary: In the 2026 Alaska Beacon voter guide questionnaire he said ICE is overfunded and tasked with unrealistic deportation goals, and that the system should maintain strong borders.
positions.quote: ICE is overfunded, under-trained, and tasked with unrealistic deportation goals.

positions.summary: In an Aug. 2026 Alaska Public Media interview he said tariffs can be a tool if used precisely, and that the tariffs imposed were not effective and raised prices.
positions.quote: It seems like we went in with a hammer and just started smashing things. To my mind, they weren’t very effective, they raised the price on lots of things.

positions.summary: In the 2026 Alaska Beacon voter guide questionnaire he said he would oppose legislation like the SAVE Act.
positions.quote: I would oppose legislation like the SAVE act as Congress should not meddle in a state’s responsibility for fair elections and it would likely make voting much harder for rural Alaskans.

candidates.researchNotes: Positions and statements come from his answers in the 2026 Alaska Beacon voter guide questionnaire and an Aug. 3, 2026 Alaska Public Media interview. The questionnaire lists him as a retired teacher who also worked about 13 years as a Forest Service forestry technician; Alaska Public Media says 15 years with the Forest Service. No campaign website was found. His answers did not address abortion, guns, taxes, minimum wage, school choice or Israel.

statements.quote: Continue to fund and support research to mitigate climate change effects.
statements.context: In the 2026 Alaska Beacon voter guide questionnaire, on climate change
